newsitem.title: USA: US power marketers jockey for generating capacity.
newsitem.headline: US power marketers jockey for generating capacity.

text.p: The race is on to capture U.S. electric generating capacity as competitors in the emerging power marketing industry jockey for position ahead of anticipated deregulation of the domestic electric grid, executives said on Wednesday.

Taking a page from deregulation of the interstate natural gas business, companies eyeing creation of national electric franchises are eyeing utility acquisitions and stakes in regional power plants, executives said in a panel talk at Cambridge Energy Research Associates annual energy forum in Houston.
"You've got to own capacity in the early stages of this immature market to do the deals you need to fill the book and let the market become liquid over time," CINergy Chairman James Rogers said .

Once deregulation opens the national electric grid to competition, the successful power marketing company will emerge with a $10 billion to $15 billion market capitalization and a base of 10 million to 15 million customers, Rogers said.

With 60 percent of industrial and utility generation capacity tied into its nationwide gas pipeline system, El Paso Energy Corp is uniquely positioned to leverage its gas pipelines to contract for generating capacity, Chairman Bill Wise said.

Even as federal and state regulators mull deregulation of the electric grid, several major power marketers have started national advertising campaigns to build name recognition ahead of retail competition.

After saying early on that control of generating capacity was not key to building a national power marketing franchise, Enron Corp executives said recently the company would build a generating portfolio. Enron is the nation's leading electric wholesaler and is on track to move $4 billion in electric power this year.

The Enron-Portland General Corp and Duke-PanEnergy mergers are hedged against the expectation retail competition will come on line years faster than most analysts had expected. "They are basically making a bet on the retail market opening up," Rogers said.

Although wholesale markets now account for about five percent of the electrons moving through the national grid, margins are already coming down as traders battle for rights to provide power to large industrial customers and municipalities seeking to trim their power bills, the executives said.

"The reality is that this market is going to be a skinny margin business" said Rogers, whose company recently snared a contract with Bristol, Tenn., which had been a Tennessee Valley Authority customer.

"Anyone who sees the market they way I do, they see prices down over time, and margins closing very quickly," he said. "The issue is how much and how fast will generation of electricity be deregulated in this country."
